According to recent reports, donald Trump, Vladimir Putin, and Xi Jinping staged a historic trilateral meeting around an enormous table on Thursday. During the APEC summit in Shenzhen, the leaders of the U.S., Russia, and China spoke for 90 minutes before issuing a "joint declaration of peace".

There's a lot to unpack about the meeting, so The Daily Show's Michael Kosta examined the major moments in the video above, starting with Trump's overtly friendly greeting with Putin.

According to recent reports, "Wow, that was chummy," remarked Kosta. "Putin's an evil dictator who we're in two proxy wars with — can you maybe not greet him like you pledged Sigma Chi together? ‘Home Alone’ Director Chris Columbus Said Minutes Before New Sequel Was Confirmed That Another Movie ‘Can’t Happen’ After Catherine O’Hara’s Death

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Chris Columbus didn’t know a new “Home Alone” was coming.
  • The director of the 1990 original spoke with Variety minutes before news broke that Disney is developing a new installment with Macaulay Culkin.
  • Industry observers note that “Catherine, as I’ve always said, is 50% of ‘Home Alone,’” Columbus states.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chris Columbus didn’t know a new “Home Alone” was coming.

The director of the 1990 original spoke with Variety minutes before news broke that Disney is developing a new installment with Macaulay Culkin. According to sources, Columbus had no knowledge that the project was in development or about to be declared. When asked about the franchise’s future, his answer was that any return faces a steep climb without Catherine O’Hara. Related Stories Maya Jama Exits ‘Love Island U.K.’ as Host After 9 Seasons: 'All Good Things Must Come to an End' Maya Jama on That Shocking 'Celebrity Traitors' Finale, [SPOILER]'s Betrayal and 'Heated' Last Roundtable: 'My Heart Was Jumping Out of My Chest'.

Industry observers note that “Catherine, as I’ve always said, is 50% of ‘Home Alone,’” Columbus states. “There’s the yin and yang of ‘Home Alone’: Catherine O’Hara and Macaulay Culkin. Without those two in the film, there is no film, because they create the emotional epicenter of that film.”.

It has been revealed that O’Hara, who played Kevin McCallister’s mother, Kate, died Jan. 30 at 71.

As reported Friday, Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg are shaping the script with Culkin and will produce through their Point Grey banner. The project is in early development at Disney, and plot details and casting remain under wraps. According to Deadline, the film grew out of a pitch Culkin made to Disney film chief David Greenbaum, told from the point of view of an older Kevin as a father.

When Variety followed up after the announcement, Columbus declined to comment further.

Columbus, who is set to receive a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame in December, was particularly warm about his former star’s return to the role in a McDonald’s holiday commercial released Nov. 17. “I love Macaulay’s McDonald’s commercial,” he claims. “Macaulay is a great actor, and I hope to work with him on something. Maybe it’ll be ‘Home Alone’-related, maybe it won’t.”.

He leaves the door open to a return built around the original ensemble.

“I think you potentially could still entertain the idea of doing another ‘Home Alone’ with the cast,” Columbus explains. “Not any of these ridiculous follow-ups to the first. And I only say ridiculous because it’s weird with filmmakers. They don’t understand why that cast works so well. It’s always about the cast. It’s like ‘The Goonies.’ It’s about the cast.”.

The franchise continued without Culkin and Columbus in “Home Alone 3” (1997), “Home Alone 4” (2002), “Home Alone: The Holiday Heist” (2012) and Disney+’s “Home Sweet Home Alone” (2021).

Industry observers note that but Columbus indicates O’Hara’s death has changed what a reunion could be. “It was really about Catherine and Macaulay, if anyone ever wanted to do a sequel,” he says, “and unfortunately that can’t happen now.”.

He also makes the case for the film’s burglars, Harry and Marv, played by Joe Pesci and Daniel Stern.

“Let’s not downsize Harry and Marv,” Columbus says. “Daniel Stern and Joe Pesci are the ultimate comic duo for that particular film. Everyone has tried in subsequent sequels to be as funny or as interesting as Dan and Joe, and they just had a chemistry that is undefinable. So you can’t do that.”.

Columbus, who also directed 1992’s “Home Alone 2: Lost in New York,” has long been skeptical of revisiting the property. In 2020, he told Insider that Disney’s planned reboot was “a waste of time” and that “nobody got in touch with me about it.” That project became “Home Sweet Home Alone.” Last year, he told Entertainment Tonight that another “Home Alone” would be a “mistake.”.

Rogen also has a personal connection to O’Hara. She played studio executive Patty Leigh in his Apple TV comedy “The Studio,” a role she still held when she died. O’Hara also spoke at Culkin’s own Walk of Fame ceremony in December 2023.

It has been revealed that columbus is next set to direct “Gremlins 3,” which is scheduled to begin shooting early next year. He executive produced Robert Eggers’ upcoming horror film “Werwulf,” which Focus Features opens Dec. 25.

This 16-Year-Old Founded an AI Missile Startup. He’s Targeting ‘Cost per Kill’

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • At 16 years old, Henrijs Dandzbergs is too young to vote.
  • In September, Dandzbergs, who was born in Latvia, was admitted to Y Combinator’s fall 2026 cohort.
  • His startup, Polemos Industries, is attempting to develop a new class of precision-guided missile that can be easily and cheaply manufactured, can be fired from portable launchers, and can resist jamming attempts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At 16 years old, Henrijs Dandzbergs is too young to vote. Or drink. Or smoke. Or drive unsupervised. But he’s not too young to win half a million dollars for his AI-guided-missile startup.

In September, Dandzbergs, who was born in Latvia, was admitted to Y Combinator’s fall 2026 cohort. The startup accelerator counts companies like Airbnb, Stripe, DoorDash, and Reddit among its alumni; Dandzbergs is likely the youngest solo founder in its vaunted history.

His startup, Polemos Industries, is attempting to develop a new class of precision-guided missile that can be easily and cheaply manufactured, can be fired from portable launchers, and can resist jamming attempts. “I think missiles are the coolest thing,” Dandzbergs tells WIRED. “A lot of people that have found success in engineering early on have had a passion for blowing stuff up.”.

In conversation, Dandzbergs is poised and articulate. He talks about “attacking hard problems,” breaking things down to “first principles,” and how the Ukraine conflict has forever altered the theater of war—a personal fixation, given his country's proximity to Russia. He projects an unassailable confidence in his own abilities.

Recent findings suggest that “He’s a pretty exceptional person,” notes Harj Taggar, a YC partner assigned to mentor Dandzbergs. “I’m still somewhat in disbelief that we’re talking about a 16-year-old.”.

Dandzbergs has resolved to apply these unusual talents to figuring out how to optimize targeted killing. His startup’s guiding ambition, according to its investor one-pager, is to bring down the “cost per kill.”.

As a young(er) kid, Dandzbergs was rarely in one place for long; his family moved between Latvia, Indonesia, Australia, and Spain. His surfer father, part owner of an insurance firm, likes to go wherever he might find the raddest waves.

Recent findings suggest that early in his schooling, which mostly took place online, Dandzbergs demonstrated a clear talent for science and math. His room started to look like a lab, littered with schematics, robotics, Raspberry Pis, and 3D-printed components.

Sources indicate that when Covid struck, Dandzbergs’ family returned to Latvia. His parents enrolled him in Astra Nova, an Elon Musk–linked school where students undergo an experimental curriculum built around lateral thinking and problem-solving instead of rote memorization. Dandzbergs took a class taught by a NASA employee and became fascinated by aerospace engineering. His lab creations became ever more elaborate: a bionic arm, a thermal control system for a model rocket, sensors for a self-flying drone.

It has been revealed that around this time, Russia invaded Ukraine. In Latvia, Dandzbergs started to see military jets overhead, and stray missiles were intercepted at the Russian border. With the sovereignty of Eastern European nations under threat, fresh defense startups began to pop up across the region. Dandzbergs wanted in.

“A patriotic intention to protect my country, European countries, and Ukrainian and American soldiers, and understanding the future of autonomous warfare—that’s my drive,” he says.

To stretch his technical skills, Dandzbergs started to take part in hackathons, where software and hardware engineers compete to develop the most sophisticated prototype from scratch.

In April of this year, he flew to London to take part in a hackathon held by Unicorn Mafia, an invitation-only group of developers. The prize included $10,000 in cash, a plane ticket to San Francisco, and free legal assistance with O-1 visa applications to stay in the US.

Industry observers note that less than 48 hours later, Dandzbergs and his two teammates, Aleksandrs Tihenko and Kai Yang, had built an AI system that could design hardware circuit boards from natural language prompts, much like how a software engineer might use AI to generate code. Though his teammates are both a few years older, Dandzbergs pushed for them to include even more intricate features in the prototype. “It was amazing,” claims Tihenko. “The imagination of Henrijs in the hardware space is just crazy.”.

In a recent development, seeing that they stood no chance of beating Dandzbergs’ group and other front-runners, teams started to drop out of the competition, according to Fergus McKenzie-Wilson, Unicorn Mafia’s director and one of the hackathon judges. “What they built was incredibly impressive,” he states. “No one had ever seen that before.”.

Industry observers note that when the organizers crowned Dandzbergs’ team victorious, somebody handed him the mic. “I’m 16 years old,” he stated.

The week after the hackathon, Dandzbergs and his teammates pitched their circuit board concept to YC. They won a place in the summer program, but Dandzbergs wavered over whether he should drop out of high school. The trio also sparred over whether the startup should focus on applying the technology to the defense sector, Dandzbergs’ primary area of interest. Dandzbergs ended up pulling out of the partnership. “It was hard,” says Tihenko. “But ultimately we just settled that the best decision for the firm would be to part ways and focus on different things.”.

In a recent development, by the summer, Danzbergs was set on building a defense startup and reapplied to YC on his own. He had spotted a gap in the market, he claimed, for AI-guided missiles that were more precise and could carry bigger warheads than the drones deployed widely in Ukraine. His products, he added, would be cheaper and easier to manufacture than hulking great rocket systems.

In a recent development, YC initially tried to steer him away. Dandzbergs was promising a lot of everything, all at once. It wasn’t clear whether his idea could work or whether pulling out of school was the right thing for him to do. “There’s a paternal element to it,” says Taggar. “You don’t want to be screwing up people's lives—and working on a startup is a pretty serious thing.”.

Dandzbergs is up against a fleet of defense companies—from Anduril to CoAspire to Leidos—aiming to develop cheaper, mass-producible missiles. The more sophisticated the guidance system, the more difficult that task becomes.

“You can build a cheap missile that doesn’t go very far. You can build a cheap missile that doesn’t carry much of a payload. You can build a cheap missile that has a low reliability rate,” says Tom Karako, director of the Missile Defense Project and senior fellow at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. “There are trade-offs.”.

It has been revealed that but Dandzbergs wasn’t going to be dissuaded, and YC figured that somebody else would probably invest in his idea. The incubator invited him to join its fall program. “Significant picture, you never know if these things are possible or not,” states Taggar. “Is it a non-zero-percent chance that it could be possible? That’s frankly the threshold, especially if it’s a really big [idea].”.

In a recent development, so far, according to Dandzbergs, Polemos Industries has developed the software system that will guide its missiles and has begun to hammer out elements of the hardware design. By the time the YC program finishes in December, he hopes to be able to showcase a prototype missile.

In a recent development, if he does ultimately succeed, though, Dandzbergs will need to confront an assortment of hairy ethical quandaries. Who should have access to these newly introduced missiles? What if a technical error were to result in friendly fire? Can he make peace with his technology being used to end somebody’s life?

According to recent reports, dandzbergs claims that he has come to terms with these complications. He says he takes solace in the belief that his motivations are pure: to protect the US and its European allies.

By his logic, autonomous weapons are an inevitable part of the future, so he might as well be the one who builds them. “I choose not to shy away from the emergence of modern conflict as a global issue. I simply don’t have a lot of respect for people that do,” he says. “I want to be part of it. I want to move with the future of warfare.”.

But others who have found themselves in a similar position say it’s difficult to know in advance how somebody will deal with the knowledge that their invention has killed people.

According to recent reports, mcKenzie-Wilson, the Unicorn Mafia director, released a drone startup in his early twenties. Initially, he had meant for the drones to evacuate wounded soldiers, but after a missile company invested, his startup retooled its technology to drop payloads too. He left around the same time.

“I don’t think I was emotionally mature enough,” he claims. “[Dandzbergs] will realize at some point. He’ll either have an issue with it or he won’t.”.

Recent findings suggest that polemos Industries unveiled itself publicly on November 5 with a glossy social media video. Set to the ticking of a clock, it featured a set of four missiles fired into the sky from ground launchers, then blowing a convoy of four military vehicles to smithereens.

The video climbed to the top of the trending page on X. In the responses, a couple of people tagged Palmer Luckey, cofounder of Anduril, who was 19 when he started his first company. “Coming for him,” Dandzbergs responded.

According to recent reports, dandzbergs recognizes that people are likely to dismiss him for his age. But he considers youth one of his biggest advantages. “Please don’t say I’m sacrificing my childhood,” he claims. “This is the childhood I dreamed of.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • United Airlines on Monday said it had resolved a "widespread system outage" that briefly affected departing flights.
  • It has been revealed that "We have resolved a technology concern that delayed flight departures," the airline noted in a statement.
  • A United spokesperson said there was no indication that the outage was a cyberattack.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

United Airlines on Monday said it had resolved a "widespread system outage" that briefly affected departing flights.

It has been revealed that "We have resolved a technology concern that delayed flight departures," the airline noted in a statement. "While some flights were delayed, there was no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights.

A United spokesperson said there was no indication that the outage was a cyberattack.

The Air Line Pilots Association, which represents pilots for United and other carriers, mentioned in an earlier message to members seen by CNBC that the operational outage was "affecting multiple pilot facing applications" and that United could not "provide outbound flights with final weights.".

United's outage came three days after a nationwide ground stop halted departures across the country for more than four hours, snarling travel and leading to widespread delays and cancellations over the weekend.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed the problems that led to Friday's ground stop on a router in Arkansas that overwhelmed systems that feed radar and other data for air traffic control. Federal Aviation Administration Administrator Bryan Bedford said the upgrades were part of "routine" maintenance to switch over from copper wires to fiber optic.

There were significantly fewer flight delays and cancellations Monday than had been reported Sunday, according to FlightAware data.

There was no indication that United's outage Monday was related to the issues that caused Friday's ground stop.

— CNBC's Leslie Josephs and Phil LeBeau contributed to this report.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The events have heightened oversight of the US tech giant and its importance to national security, as well as wiping several hundred billion dollars off the stock market valuation of what investors treat as the world's most valuable organization in the space of a month.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nvidia on Tuesday mentioned it had created a board-level national security and export-control committee.

This follows the scandal surrounding former CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned last week over extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected of spying for China and working to help ensure higher quality chips crucial to AI development made it to the Chinese market.

The events have heightened oversight of the US tech giant and its importance to national security, as well as wiping several hundred billion dollars off the stock market valuation of what investors treat as the world's most valuable organization in the space of a month.

According to recent reports, since Huang's resignation, some investors — including Elon Musk and Donald Trump — have voiced concern that his departure could leave Nvidia and America's AI sector in peril and are now calling for his return. Huang on Tuesday, expressed regret for "serious mistakes" in his personal life before declaring he would be "honored" to return if the company's board of directors thought that was "in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America.".

Nvidia is calling the new group its National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee.

Suzanne Nora Johnson, a former vice chair at Goldman Sachs, will chair the committee, joined by fellow directors Stephen Neal, a former CEO of a law firm, John Dabiri, a professor of aeronautics and mechanical engineering at the California Institute of Technology (Caltech).

The committee will meet at least once every quarter. It will also incorporate independent legal, national security and trade compliance experts.

Nvidia already has a lower-level National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team; these groups will report to the board-level committee.

"We are committed to working constructively with government and industry partners to help establish and advance a robust framework that uses every tool at our disposal to safeguard national security while supporting continued technological innovation," Board Chair Harvey Jones noted in a statement.

The tech giant did not explicitly link the decision to November's developments and Huang's rapid fall from grace, but the timing seemed conspicuous.

The decision was declared hours ahead of Nvidia publishing its third-quarter results, with its still-stratospheric share price having fallen roughly 28% in the past month.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

US President Donald Trump, whom Huang was influential in persuading to allow the export of better-quality Nvidia chips to China than other US companies and officials deemed prudent, welcomed Nvidia's move on arrival in the Philippines on Tuesday.

"Yes, that's a good idea. It's a great company," he noted during a photo opportunity at a Manila meeting with the other "Quad" leaders from Australia, India and Japan. "It's a great idea.".

Trump reportedly owned Nvidia stock worth tens of millions of dollars before the share price fell. He also owns shares in other big tech companies.

Recent findings suggest that huang resigned last week after admitting to extramarital affairs in a message to Nvidia employees. This followed widespread reports, seemingly based on US and other intelligence, that one of the affairs was with a woman who used to lead a Singapore-based cloud computing firm.

Sources indicate that that tech giant, Megaspseed International, is a major Nvidia client and is suspected of diverting advanced chips to China in violation of US export controls. Intelligence officials also suspect Huang's partner of being an asset of Chinese intelligence services.

The reporting on the case also seems to show these suspicions had been known to US officials and other countries, including Singapore, for roughly a year.

A material just one atom thick reveals a strange quantum secret

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (545 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that scientists at the University of Osaka in Japan have made a significant discovery in quantum physics, directly observing an unusual electronic state forming where a material just one atom thick meets a metal.
  • In a recent development, to investigate this behavior, the researchers produced a carefully controlled, single atomic layer of ytterbium and copper (YbCu2) on the surface of a copper crystal.
  • The experiments uncovered two separate heavy fermion states with different characteristics.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that scientists at the University of Osaka in Japan have made a significant discovery in quantum physics, directly observing an unusual electronic state forming where a material just one atom thick meets a metal. Known as a heavy fermion state, this phenomenon causes electrons to behave as though they have much greater mass than normal. These states are associated with extraordinary quantum effects, including unconventional superconductivity, and the discovery could provide a latest way to develop materials with unusual electronic properties.

In a recent development, to investigate this behavior, the researchers produced a carefully controlled, single atomic layer of ytterbium and copper (YbCu2) on the surface of a copper crystal. They then used powerful synchrotron light to study the electrons and their interactions at the boundary between the two materials. The results demonstrated that electrons confined to the thin atomic layer could interact with freely moving electrons in the copper beneath it, producing the unusual heavy fermion behavior.

Two Distinct Quantum States Emerge.

The experiments uncovered two separate heavy fermion states with different characteristics. One existed primarily within the two-dimensional atomic layer, while the other reached beyond that layer and into the three-dimensional copper crystal below.

According to recent reports, the second state was particularly vital because it provided the first direct evidence of heavy fermion behavior generated by interactions across such an interface. Researchers traced the effect to the mixing, or hybridization, of localized ytterbium 4f electrons in the atomic layer with mobile conduction electrons inside the copper substrate. This interaction demonstrated how combining materials with different electronic characteristics can produce quantum behavior that neither material would necessarily exhibit on its own.

In a recent development, "This achievement was made possible by our continued efforts to create high-quality materials and measure their electronic states as precisely as possible," notes senior author Professor Shin-ichi Kimura. "Our next goal is to engineer and control such heavy-electron states, opening the way to previously unexplored quantum states, including unconventional superconductivity.".

A Newly introduced Approach to Designing Quantum Materials.

Sources indicate that the discovery suggests that the boundaries between materials could become powerful tools for creating and controlling exotic quantum states. Rather than relying only on the properties of individual substances, scientists may be able to develop entirely fresh electronic behaviors by carefully selecting and combining ultrathin atomic layers with suitable underlying materials.

In a recent development, future research could focus on adjusting the structures of these interfaces, controlling the electronic orbitals involved, and manipulating moiré patterns that arise when atomic arrangements overlap. Such approaches may allow researchers to produce and fine-tune quantum phenomena in materials with extremely small dimensions, including effects that cannot be achieved in conventional materials. Ultimately, this could open upcoming possibilities for engineering advanced quantum materials and investigating unconventional superconductivity.

Materials provided by The University of Osaka. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that editor’s Note:  Call to Earth is a CNN editorial series committed to reporting on the environmental challenges facing our planet, together with the solutions.
  • Sources indicate that originally a term used by trophy hunters in Africa, the “Big Five” described the animals most challenging to shoot and kill: the lion, elephant, leopard, rhino, and buffalo.
  • According to recent reports, however, British photographer Graeme Green has reclaimed the narrative, creating a global “Upcoming Substantial Five” for wildlife photography.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that editor’s Note:  Call to Earth is a CNN editorial series committed to reporting on the environmental challenges facing our planet, together with the solutions. Rolex’s Perpetual Planet initiative has partnered with CNN to drive awareness and education around key sustainability issues and to inspire positive action.

Sources indicate that originally a term used by trophy hunters in Africa, the “Big Five” described the animals most challenging to shoot and kill: the lion, elephant, leopard, rhino, and buffalo. Nowadays, it is more loosely used to refer to some of Africa’s largest and most iconic animals.

According to recent reports, however, British photographer Graeme Green has reclaimed the narrative, creating a global “Upcoming Substantial Five” for wildlife photography. In 2021, 50,000 people around the world voted for the five animals they would most like to photograph, or see photographed, in the wild. Five animals were crowned the winners: the elephant, polar bear, lion, gorilla and tiger.

This week, sees the publication of “The Newly introduced Massive 5” photography book, which features images of those animals and other at-risk wildlife, from photography legends such as Ami Vitale, Steve McCurry and Paul Nicklen, and essays from famous conservationists and activists including like Jane Goodall and Paula Kahumbu.

Green says that the book celebrates wildlife and is a global call to action on complications impacting wildlife, including habitat loss, poaching, pollution and climate change.

Green was on assignment in Botswana at least a decade ago when he came up with the idea for a project to encourage people to “shoot with a camera, not a gun,” he notes.

“I thought this would be a way to get people really focusing on wildlife, thinking about the wildlife they love, thinking about the animals that are at risk.”.

Ten photographs that made the world wake up to climate change.

In total, the book includes the work of 144 globally renowned wildlife photographers from Ecuador to India. Curating the images took nearly two years of work, notes Green.

According to recent reports, “I think these are some of the most beautiful and creative images that I’ve seen put together in one book,” says Green. “These are the species that we are at risk of losing.”.

According to the UN, nature is declining at an unprecedented rate, with around one million of the planet’s animal and plant species facing extinction. The “Upcoming Substantial 5,” all of which are threatened, act as ambassadors for what is happening in the natural world, states Green.

As well as being a powerful reminder of what we stand to lose, the book also points people towards potential solutions. Featured essays explore the benefits of rewilding and the importance of indigenous communities in conservation.

A chapter on endangered species from bees to blue whales illustrates the alarming threat climate change poses to animals outside of the “New Major 5.” “That’s only the tip of the iceberg – I could have included thousands of pictures because that’s how serious the situation is,” says Green.

Why a wildlife photographer took 40,000 photos to capture these extraordinary birds.

Jane Goodall, a leading conservationist who also wrote the afterword to the book, mentioned in a press release that “we have a window of time during which we can start to heal some of the harm we have inflicted on the natural world, but only if we get together and take action now.

“I hope the photos will lead people into the wonderful worlds of these iconic species. Then, perhaps, other people will become involved in helping to create a world where wildlife can flourish for future generations to enjoy,” she said.

“The Fresh Big 5: A Global Photography Project For Endangered Wildlife,” by Graeme Green, published by Earth Aware Editions, is on sale from April 4, 2023.

This story has been updated to reflect the range of concerns covered by the book.

  • “Michael,” Antoine Fuqua’s billion-dollar portrait of the King of Pop, will not be submitted for the 2027 EE BAFTA Film Awards, Variety has learned exclusively.
  • According to recent reports, according to sources with direct knowledge, producer Graham King, Fuqua and various stakeholders made the call after consulting with Lionsgate, international distributor Universal Pictures and the film’s other partners.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The highest-grossing biopic ever made is sitting out one of the biggest stops on the road to the Oscars.

“Michael,” Antoine Fuqua’s billion-dollar portrait of the King of Pop, will not be submitted for the 2027 EE BAFTA Film Awards, Variety has learned exclusively. That takes actors like Jaafar Jackson and Colman Domingo, along with the film’s entire craft team, out of the running before longlist voting begins. Related Stories Maya Jama Strikes Deal With Netflix (EXCLUSIVE) Maya Jama Exits ‘Love Island U.K.’ as Host After 9 Seasons: 'All Good Things Must Come to an End'.

According to recent reports, according to sources with direct knowledge, producer Graham King, Fuqua and various stakeholders made the call after consulting with Lionsgate, international distributor Universal Pictures and the film’s other partners. The sources cite “multiple factors” behind the decision but declined to say what they are.

Representatives for Lionsgate, Universal Pictures and GK Films declined to comment.

Sources tell Variety that Lionsgate and Universal supports the filmmakers’ decision.

Earlier this month, the organization sent film voting members its Recommended Viewing Groups for the 2027 awards, which divides every entered film into 15 groups. Each member is randomly assigned one. The British Academy encourages voters to watch as many entries as they can but asks those short on time to prioritize their assigned group and the films in their specialist craft category. “Michael” isn’t in any of them.

BAFTA’s Stage Two entry and deadline passed Nov. 19. A draft list of entered films goes out to entrants and members Nov. 26. The final list will be published on Dec. 4, the same morning Round One voting opens to set the longlists.

Among the films that entered are “The Odyssey,” “Artificial,” “Behemoth!,” “Project Hail Mary,” “Wuthering Heights” and “The Social Reckoning.” The year’s other box office heavyweights, “The Super Mario Galaxy Movie” and “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” are also in the mix, along with two music documentaries, “Epic: Elvis Presley in Concert” and “Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger.”.

It’s an unusual move for a film that has spent the fall building an awards case.

The 80th BAFTA Film Awards reclaim its traditional spot ahead of the Academy this season. Last year, the British Academy announced nominations five days after the Oscars did, breaking a pattern that had held since 2001. This time, longlists arrive Jan. 7 and nominations Jan. 19, two days before the Academy unveils its own on Jan. 21. The London ceremony follows Feb. 21, three weeks ahead of the March 14 Oscars at the Dolby Theatre. For voters on both sides of the Atlantic, the BAFTA ballot is the first real read on the Oscar race, especially given the Academy’s large international voting bloc.

Sources indicate that it’s also a departure from producer King’s own playbook. “Bohemian Rhapsody,” his last music biopic, won Rami Malek the BAFTA for leading actor on the way to four Oscars, which he repeated.

King has criticized the British Academy before. After February’s ceremony, Tourette’s syndrome campaigner John Davidson involuntarily shouted the N-word while “Sinners” stars Michael B. Jordan and Delroy Lindo presented the night’s first award, and the BBC aired the slur despite a two-hour tape delay. Both organizations apologized.

Recent findings suggest that “For years, BAFTA and the BBC have repeatedly displayed cultural insensitivity and tone deafness,” King said at the time in a statement posted to his GK Films’ Instagram account. “Their inability to take accountability for their actions or inactions is reckless and unacceptable.”.

The sources did not say whether the episode factored into this year’s decision.

The news also comes after the Golden Globes rejected the studio’s bid to place “Michael” in the comedy or musical categories, a submission that came with a letter from Fuqua, pushing the film into the more crowded drama race. An FYC screening at the DGA reportedly drew a standing ovation.

Industry observers note that at the Gotham Awards on Nov. 30, Fuqua, King, Jaafar Jackson, Colman Domingo and Nia Long will accept the Musical Tribute Award.

The commercial case was settled months ago, with a sequel at the moment in development.

Industry observers note that “Michael” opened in April to $97 million domestically and $217 million worldwide, a record debut for a music biopic. In July, it became the first biopic to cross $1 billion globally. It’s Lionsgate’s biggest release ever, topping the $865 million of “The Hunger Games: Catching Fire” and the studio notes it’s the first film from an independent distributor to reach the milestone.

Sources indicate that the critics’ reception was much harsher than audiences’. The film right now holds a 38% score on Rotten Tomatoes. However, viewers have consistently singled out Jaafar Jackson’s star-making turn as his uncle; audiences gave it an A- CinemaScore.

Recent findings suggest that written by John Logan, “Michael” traces Jackson’s rise from the Jackson 5 in the 1960s through the Bad World Tour in the late 1980s, closing before the first allegations of misconduct became public in 1993. Jaafar Jackson leads a cast that includes Domingo as Joseph Jackson, Long as Katherine Jackson, Miles Teller as attorney John Branca and Mike Myers as record executive Walter Yetnikoff.

In a recent development, skipping BAFTA doesn’t affect the film’s Oscar eligibility, and the Globes, Critics Choice Awards and guild circuits remain in play. But it gives up one of the season’s biggest televised platforms, along with one of the few chances for a breakout performance to reach an international voting body before Oscar nominations voting opens.

Whether the decision ultimately costs “Michael” a trip to the Oscars remains to be seen.

#47665. Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1294 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1294 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, an eight-year study of children in Finland has revealed a surprising connection between screen time and brain function.
  • The findings suggest that the amount of time children spend in front of screens may be less important than how they use that time.
  • In a recent development, the discovery comes amid growing concerns about insufficient physical activity among teenagers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, an eight-year study of children in Finland has revealed a surprising connection between screen time and brain function. Researchers found that children who spent more time using screens tended to have better cognitive processing abilities as teenagers, challenging the widespread assumption that screen time is necessarily harmful to developing brains.

The findings suggest that the amount of time children spend in front of screens may be less important than how they use that time. Activities that encourage learning, creativity, and problem-solving could be particularly valuable. Researchers emphasize that the goal should not be to eliminate screen time, but to balance it with physical activity and mentally stimulating experiences.

In a recent development, the discovery comes amid growing concerns about insufficient physical activity among teenagers. A sedentary lifestyle has been linked to poorer academic performance, while regular exercise is known to support brain function, particularly in adults. However, scientists still have much to learn about how physical activity, sitting, and screen use during childhood influence thinking abilities later in adolescence.

Sources indicate that these questions are especially vital because childhood and adolescence are critical periods of brain development. Changes in attention, memory, and learning during these years can have lasting consequences, potentially influencing educational opportunities and career paths well into adulthood.

It has been revealed that to investigate these relationships, Finnish researchers examined how screen time, physical activity, and sedentary behavior from childhood through adolescence were associated with cognitive performance in teenagers. They also explored whether the connections differed between boys and girls and whether the intensity of physical activity made a difference.

More Screen Time Linked to Better Thinking Skills.

One of the study's most unexpected findings was that greater screen time throughout childhood was associated with better cognitive processing in adolescence.

Sources indicate that cognitive processing refers to the mental abilities people use to take in information, pay attention, remember details, learn latest things, and solve problems. These abilities play an crucial role in school performance and everyday decision-making.

Industry observers note that the findings challenge the idea that all screen time should be viewed as harmful. However, the researchers caution that the relationship may depend on what children are actually doing while using digital devices. Watching videos, playing games that require strategic thinking, and engaging in educational activities may involve very different levels of mental effort.

Sources indicate that "The findings suggest that screen time can support children's and adolescents' cognitive processing. Presumably, the essential point here is what kind of things they do in their screen time. Teachers and parents should encourage children to use devices and screens in such ways that promote active thinking, problem-solving, creativity, and learning," states Doctoral Researcher Petri Jalanko from the University of Jyväskylä.

"We should not regard screen time solely as harmful but seek balance between physical activity and screen time that promotes active thinking," Jalanko summarizes.

Exercise Affects Boys' and Girls' Brains Differently.

The researchers also uncovered a more complicated picture of how physical activity relates to thinking and memory.

Recent findings suggest that among girls, spending more time engaged in light-intensity physical activity since childhood was associated with better working memory during adolescence. For boys, greater participation in guided physical activity over the same period was linked to stronger working memory.

Working memory is the brain's ability to temporarily hold and use information. It allows someone to remember instructions while completing a task, keep track of numbers during mental calculations, or follow a conversation while processing newly introduced information.

Sources indicate that light-intensity physical activity generally includes relatively gentle movements that do not substantially increase breathing or heart rate. Guided physical activity refers to exercise carried out with some form of instruction or supervision, such as organized sports or structured exercise sessions.

The differences between boys and girls suggest that the relationship between exercise and brain health may depend on more than simply how much a person moves. The type of activity, how it is organized, and the individual's sex could all play a role.

Another Surprising Finding About Physical Activity.

According to recent reports, the study produced another counterintuitive result. Teenagers who reported spending less time in unsupervised physical activity tended to perform better on measures of cognitive processing.

Yet when researchers used wearable sensors to objectively measure movement and heart rate, they found no association between overall physical activity or sedentary time and cognitive performance.

According to recent reports, one possible explanation is that wearable devices measure movement without revealing what a person is actually doing. For example, a sensor may record periods of sitting or physical activity, but it cannot determine whether someone is solving a difficult problem, studying, participating in an organized activity, or simply resting.

This distinction could help explain why questionnaire responses revealed relationships that were not apparent in the sensor measurements.

It has been revealed that "Our study indicates that the connections of physical activity and sedentary behavior to cognitive processing are complex and depend on the sex, the type and assessment method of physical activity and sedentary time. Moreover, boys and girls may benefit from different types of physical activity in view of brain health," Jalanko adds.

Recent findings suggest that "However, we need more intervention studies to find out causal relations and sex differences in this respect. Moreover, it is crucial to examine more specifically the effects of the intensity of physical activity on changes taking place in cognitive processing.".

What the Eight-Year Study Revealed.

The findings come from an eight-year follow-up conducted as part of the PANIC study, a long-running Finnish research project investigating children's physical activity and nutrition.

Industry observers note that the current analysis included 260 participants, consisting of 124 girls and 136 boys. Their average age at the adolescent assessment was 15.8 years.

Sources indicate that researchers collected information about physical activity and sedentary behavior using both questionnaires and wearable devices that combined heart rate monitoring with movement measurements. This approach allowed them to compare participants' reported activities with data collected by sensors.

To evaluate cognitive abilities, the researchers used the CogState test battery, a collection of computerized assessments designed to measure aspects of mental performance. The tests examined learning, attention, and working memory.

Importantly, the findings show associations rather than cause and effect. They do not establish that increasing screen time will improve a child's thinking abilities or that reducing certain types of exercise will produce cognitive benefits. Intervention studies, in which researchers deliberately change participants' activities and measure the results, are needed to determine whether these relationships are causal.

Recent findings suggest that nevertheless, the results offer an key perspective on the continuing debate over children's screen use. Rather than treating all time spent with digital devices as equally harmful, the researchers suggest paying closer attention to whether those activities encourage active thinking and learning.

The research also highlights the importance of considering different forms of physical activity rather than focusing exclusively on the total amount of exercise children receive.

Together, the findings suggest that supporting healthy brain development may require a more nuanced approach, one that combines physical activity with opportunities for learning, creativity, and mental engagement, including those that take place on screens.

The study was published in the scientific journal Pediatric Exercise Science.

Latest Update: Disney beats fourth-quarter estimates, targets $3 billion in savings through cost-cutting efforts

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1161 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Disney on Tuesday reported quarterly earnings and revenue that exceeded analysts' expectations and announced it's targeting $3 billion in cost savings by fiscal 2029.
  • Those cost-cutting efforts include several rounds of layoffs announced in recent months, Disney's chief financial officer, Hugh Johnston, told CNBC.
  • Future cost-saving measures will include reductions in administrative and other general expenses, Johnston said, while adding, "We do expect more layoffs.".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Disney on Tuesday reported quarterly earnings and revenue that exceeded analysts' expectations and announced it's targeting $3 billion in cost savings by fiscal 2029.

Those cost-cutting efforts include several rounds of layoffs announced in recent months, Disney's chief financial officer, Hugh Johnston, told CNBC. The most recent round, which seeks to reduce costs by up to 20%, was reported earlier this month.

Future cost-saving measures will include reductions in administrative and other general expenses, Johnston said, while adding, "We do expect more layoffs.".

Disney CEO Josh D'Amaro told investors on the tech giant's earnings call that the job cuts are "not easy.".

It has been revealed that "They affect people who care deeply about Disney and have contributed so much to this organization," he said. "At the same time, these steps are notable if we want to be a company that moves faster, adapts to a rapidly changing environment, and keeps investing in the content and technology that will drive our growth.".

The cuts will help Disney fund its $26 billion in projected content spend for fiscal 2027, a 9% increase from fiscal 2026.

The entertainment giant is also forecasting double-digit growth in earnings per share in the next fiscal year, as well as segment operating income growth of around 8%.

Disney noted that the majority of that growth will be concentrated in the first half of the year due to the theatrical debut of "Avengers: Doomsday" and a boost from the Super Bowl, which will air on Disney's ESPN and ABC networks.

It has been revealed that "The growth is really going to come in the first half of this year," Johnston mentioned. "That's the opposite of what we saw in '26, where the growth was backloaded.".

The firm will also increase its annual dividend to $2 a share, a 33% increase from the previously declared dividend. It will be payable in two installments of $1 per share, one in January and one in July.

Here's how Disney performed in its fiscal fourth quarter ended Oct. 3, compared with what Wall Street expected, according to LSEG:.

Disney reported net income for the fiscal fourth quarter of $2.61 billion, or $1.51 per share, compared with $1.31 billion, or 73 cents per share, during the same period the year prior.

Adjusting for one-time items, including severance and other restructuring charges as well as the value of intangible assets, Disney reported earnings per share of $1.77.

The company's revenue for the quarter was 16% higher year over year, and results were once again lifted by its parks and streaming divisions.

Disney's experiences segment, which includes its theme parks and cruises, reported nearly $10.11 billion in revenue, up 15% year over year. Operating income for the unit increased 20% to $2.25 billion.

The division is already a top performer for the company, but it benefited in the fiscal fourth quarter because of an extra calendar week compared with the previous fiscal year.

While international attendance continues to lag at Disney's domestic parks, it is being offset by domestic attendance, especially at the Walt Disney World resort in Orlando, Florida, Johnston said.

Growth at Disneyland Paris was driven by recent investments including an expansion area called World of Frozen. Attendance at the Hong Kong and Shanghai parks remained soft because of broad economic challenges in those regions, according to Disney.

Still, D'Amaro said he believes the growth in parks will be sustainable through next year, especially with fresh additions, including the "Monsters, Inc."-themed land "Monstropolis" opening at Walt Disney World in 2027.

"Q1 forward resort bookings at Walt Disney World are pacing up compared to the prior year," he noted. "And upcoming capacity and new experiences will start coming online in 2027. We keep investing to make the experience fresh, and what we see is that drives repeat visits.".

The company expects operating income for the experiences segment to grow in the high-single digits in fiscal 2027. Growth is expected to be front-loaded as the company laps the launch of the Disney Adventure cruise ship, which set sail in March.

According to recent reports, over at its entertainment division, Disney saw revenue increase 17% to $11.89 billion. Operating income nearly doubled to $1.33 billion.

Revenue from streaming, specifically, rose 19% to $6.1 billion, Disney remarked.

The segment benefited from the extra week on the fiscal calendar as well as from growth in subscription and affiliate fees. Additionally, the organization saw higher theatrical distribution revenue from titles like "Toy Story 5.".

Disney mentioned Tuesday it expects operating income for the entertainment division to grow in the high-single digits in the coming fiscal year.

The manufacturer's sports division saw revenue increase 16% in the fiscal fourth quarter, reaching $4.61 billion. Operating income for the segment surged more than 50% to $1.39 billion.

Subscription and affiliate fees fueled this growth alongside an increase in advertising revenue.

The company expects its sports division's operating income to grow by double digits in fiscal 2027. It noted that the fiscal first quarter of the year will see some declines because of the timing of College Football Playoff games and the Latest Year's window. However, the fiscal second quarter will benefit from the college championship as well as the broadcast of Super Bowl 61.

Disney's outlook for overall and segment results for fiscal 2027 excludes the impact of a 53rd week in fiscal 2026.

According to recent reports, D'Amaro has made advancing technology a pillar of the organization's growth strategy. In September, Disney hired Karandeep Anand in the newly created position of chief technology officer.

It has been revealed that "Technology is central to how we connect fans to more of Disney and drive returns on our investment," D'Amaro said on the earnings call. "[Anand has] been energized by how much opportunity he sees to move faster and go further in product and technology. Done right, that means serving our fans even better, working more efficiently and being more innovative across every one of our businesses.".

Disney revealed a partnership with Adobe earlier this month to develop generative artificial intelligence models.

D'Amaro told investors that the team is exploring ways to use AI to make booking trips to Disney parks easier.

It has been revealed that "There's actually a vacation planning tool that's in beta right now at Walt Disney World. We built that with our partners at Google, and I've had a chance to experiment with it myself," he said. "It'll be incredibly helpful for our guests who are booking trips. With these AI features, it can feel like you've got someone sitting right by your side, like a personal concierge, that aims and responds to the way that you want to actually book your trip to Walt Disney World.".

The entertainment tech giant has also expanded its short-form content, adding a vertical video channel within the Disney+ mobile app. The company had previously announced a partnership with TikTok to bring creator content to the streaming app.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) ruled against Turkey over the detention of human rights lawyer and elected lawmaker Can Atalay.
  • The ECHR published its decision on Tuesday, saying that Turkey must release Atalay and allow him to take up his seat in the Turkish parliament.
  • The court ruled that his continued detention had been intended to silence him and undermine political pluralism.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) ruled against Turkey over the detention of human rights lawyer and elected lawmaker Can Atalay.

The ECHR published its decision on Tuesday, saying that Turkey must release Atalay and allow him to take up his seat in the Turkish parliament.

The court ruled that his continued detention had been intended to silence him and undermine political pluralism.

It ordered Turkey to pay him €32,500 (about $35,700) in compensation.

The judges stressed that Atalay's case should not be considered separately, but rather in the wider context of the detention of political opponents, human rights activists and journalists in Turkey.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Turkey was among the original signatories of the European Convention on Human Rights. Yet it has previously refused to comply with the court's decisions in the cases of rights activist Osman Kavala and prominent Kurdish politician Selahattin Demirtas.

As a lawyer, Atalay represented victims in numerous social and political cases in Turkey, as well as in freedom of speech cases involving journalists and writers.

He was also among the leading voices in the 2013 Gezi protests, which the government called an attempted coup.

Because of his involvement in the protests, Atalay, along with seven others, was sentenced to 18 years in prison in April 2022 for "aiding and abetting an attempted coup.".

Continuing his struggle from the infamous Silivri prison, Atalay ran as a candidate for the Workers' Party of Turkey (TIP) in the 2023 parliamentary elections.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

A candidate for the earthquake-hit province of Hatay, he won his seat but was denied release despite multiple rulings by the Constitutional Court, Turkey's top court.

His parliamentary status was revoked in 2024, a decision the Constitutional Court later overturned. President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's party stopped the opposition from formally reading the decision in parliament.

Although a year later an opposition lawmaker read the decision in parliament, Atalay remains in jail.

After the ECHR's ruling was published, TIP leader Erkan Bas took to social media to call for Atalay's release and the restoration of his parliamentary mandate.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The CMA Awards‘ producers knew it; they knew her.
  • In a recent development, with help from Swift’s performance of a “I Knew It, I Knew You”/”Our Song” medley, the CMAs had their highest overall viewership in seven years, ABC declared.
  • According to recent reports, not every bit of that increase necessarily had to do with Swift.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Senior Music Writer and Chief Music Critic.

The CMA Awards‘ producers knew it; they knew her. What they undoubtedly knew was that a performance by Taylor Swift would bring a ratings bonanza to the 60th annual telecast, with the only question being how major a boost. It was a substantial one, as ratings released Friday indicated the 2026 show being up 26% in total viewers and an even more impressive 55% gain in the key 18-49 demo, versus the previous year’s tallies.

In a recent development, with help from Swift’s performance of a “I Knew It, I Knew You”/”Our Song” medley, the CMAs had their highest overall viewership in seven years, ABC declared. The show drew 7.62 total viewers, versus 6.03 million in 2025, for that 26% increase. The 18-49 share of the audience, where the 55% growth was found, had the telecast earning a 1.01 rating, compared to a 0.65 share last year. Related Stories Maya Jama Strikes Deal With Netflix (EXCLUSIVE) Maya Jama on That Shocking 'Celebrity Traitors' Finale, [SPOILER]'s Betrayal and 'Heated' Last Roundtable: 'My Heart Was Jumping Out of My Chest'.

According to recent reports, not every bit of that increase necessarily had to do with Swift. America has certainly been high on Ella Langley, who did at least as well as anticipated in the awards, sweeping nearly every category she was up for to win a record six CMA Awards. Her “Choosin’ Texas” song is at the moment enjoying its 28th week atop Billboard’s Hot 100 chart, an all-time record — although Langley chose to sing a different song on the telecast, her latest single, “Loving Life Again.” (The singer’s performance of the then-new “Choosin’ Texas” on the CMAs last year has been cited by her label as giving the hit its biggest turbo boost.).

Also possibly a factor in viewer anticipation for the show was the promise of a Dolly Parton tribute. The show opened with host Lainey Wilson and Vince Gill dueting on “I Will Always Love You,” a scaled-down but still very well-received homage, in comparison to the all-star Parton tribute special the Country Music Association and ABC put on in October. Other stars on the show included country drawing powers like Kacey Musgraves, Miranda Lambert, Tucker Wetmore, Chris Stapleton, Megan Moroney, Luke Combs and what turned out to be a controversial hard-rock salute to Brooks & Dunn.

Recent findings suggest that but without a doubt, the increase would not have been in such remarkable double-digits range without Swift. A previous Variety report, “Taylor Swift’s CMA Return Helped Disney Sell More Ads,” noted that ABC even re-opened its previously closed advertising space for the three-hour telecast after Swift officially signed on with a performance.

In a recent development, the superstar had declared that she would be attending the show as soon as the nominations came in, with Swift landing one for her Disney/Pixar “Toy Story 5” closing theme song. But the fact that she would be performing was not revealed until days before the show. Swift last performed on the CMA Awards telecast in 2013; she last made an appearance on the show in 2016.

Swift made her performance an all-star affair, beginning the number with a pre-taped and highly choreographed trip through the backstage area that had her meticulously interacting with Brooks & Dunn, Lainey Wilson, Eric Church, Sugarland, Little Major Town and Brad Paisley, all of whom she has some kind of history with. Then, with a symbolic toss back and forth with Bill Anderson, the longest-serving Grand Ole Opry member, it kicked to the live performance and she took to a “Toy Story”-themed set to complete the number, with Keith Urban on ganjo, throwing in a snippet of her first country No. 1 from 20 years ago, “Our Song.”.

Later in the show, she presented a lifetime achievement award to Brooks & Dunn.

The CMAs telecast on Wednesday evening was preceded the night before on ABC by a preview show, “Darius, Dolly and 60 Years of Celebration: Countdown to the CMAs with Robin Roberts.” That Tuesday broadcast picked up 2.99 million total viewers, getting a 0.29 rating among adults 18-49 and a 0.38 among adults 25-54.

Sources indicate that the CMAs marked Swift’s first public performance of “I Knew It, I Knew You,” after she’d previously sung it at the Motion Picture Academy’s governors ball and at private awards-circuit showcases. It may not be the last the public sees and hears of Swift doing it. She was just nominated this week for a Grammy for song of the year for the film theme, and is hoping to be nominated for a best song Oscar for the first time. It’s likely both Grammys producers and Oscar producers will be hoping for their own Swift mashups, although a possible nomination for the Academy Awards is still two months away.

The 60th CMA Awards delivered their largest TV audience of the decade.

It has been revealed that the Nov. 18 awards averaged 7.62 million viewers on ABC and Disney+, the best same-day total for the awards since 2019 (when it brought in more than 11 million viewers). Wednesday’s show finished just ahead of the 7.57 million viewers for the 2022 awards — with the caveat that Nielsen has made several changes to the way it measures ratings in the years since then.

Industry observers note that the CMA Awards drew a 1.01 rating among adults 18-49 (equivalent to about 1.37 million people in the demographic), the first time the show has cleared a 1.0 rating since 2022. The telecast grew by 26 percent in viewers and 55 percent in adults 18-49 from a year ago (6.04 million viewers, 0.65 rating in the 18-49 demo). In a recent development, ella Langley set a record with six wins at the awards, including entertainer of the year. Her long-running No. 1 hit “Choosin’ Texas” won CMA Awards for song, single and music video of the year.

#47657. Autistic brains look surprisingly similar on average. Then scientists looked closer.

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (766 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Autistic brains look surprisingly similar on average. Then scientists looked closer.

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (766 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Brain scans have revealed a surprising pattern in people with autism.
  • The findings, published in JNeurosci, suggest that looking at average brain activity may conceal important differences among people with autism spectrum disorder (ASD).
  • The research was led by Dorit Kliemann and James Traer of the University of Iowa, who worked with collaborators to investigate how brain activity differs between adults with and without autism.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Brain scans have revealed a surprising pattern in people with autism. Although adults with and without autism showed remarkably similar brain activity when researchers compared group averages, a closer examination uncovered striking differences between individuals. These differences were especially pronounced in brain regions involved in understanding and responding to social information.

The findings, published in JNeurosci, suggest that looking at average brain activity may conceal important differences among people with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). The discovery could help scientists better understand why autism varies so widely from person to person and eventually support more personalized approaches to care.

The research was led by Dorit Kliemann and James Traer of the University of Iowa, who worked with collaborators to investigate how brain activity differs between adults with and without autism.

What Brain Scans Reveal When People Watch Movies.

Recent findings suggest that to explore these differences, the team examined previously collected brain imaging data from Indiana University and Caltech. The recordings captured brain activity as adults with and without autism watched movies from several genres, including animation, action, romantic comedy, and Hitchcockian thrillers.

Movies offered researchers a way to study how the brain responds to a constantly changing stream of sights, sounds, and social interactions. Unlike simple laboratory tasks, movies present a rich mixture of information that more closely resembles the complexity of everyday experiences.

Using the imaging data, the researchers trained a computational model to identify connections between brain activity and different elements of the movies. These included visual details, sounds, and more abstract social information, such as interactions between characters.

After training, the model was able to accurately predict activity across several brain systems.

Kliemann explained why this approach is particularly useful for investigating the social challenges sometimes associated with autism: "The computational model allowed us to look for robust brain responses to many different aspects of the complex, dynamic contexts in the movies.".

A Surprising Difference Hidden by Brain Activity Averages.

The most unexpected finding emerged when researchers compared the two groups.

Sources indicate that at first, the results suggested relatively little difference. When brain responses were averaged across participants, the model predicted activity in various brain systems similarly for adults with and without autism.

However, the picture changed when the researchers examined how much individual participants differed from others in their own group.

It has been revealed that people with autism showed substantially greater variation in their brain responses than participants without autism. In other words, although the overall group averages looked similar, the responses of individual autistic participants were much less alike.

Recent findings suggest that this increased variability appeared across nearly every brain system examined. The strongest differences occurred in the social brain system, a network of regions involved in processing social information and understanding other people.

Why the Findings Could Change Autism Research.

The results raise important questions about how scientists investigate autism. Many existing approaches to understanding and treating the condition rely heavily on comparing average measurements from groups of autistic and nonautistic individuals.

But if autistic people show considerable differences in how their brains process information, these averages may obscure some of the most meaningful findings.

Traer described the team's surprise: "We were surprised by the similarity of group averages. The results suggest that we need to focus on understanding the details of individual brain responses. How and why do they differ?".

Rather than searching only for brain activity patterns shared by everyone with autism, the findings point toward the potential value of studying individuals and identifying smaller groups with similar characteristics.

Kliemann highlighted what this could mean for future research and support: "Identifying ASD subgroups may help us build a more precise understanding of the condition and help develop ways to provide individually tailored support.".

The researchers now plan to investigate how these differences in brain activity relate to variations in autism-related behavior. They hope to determine where and when the differences emerge, how they are connected to individual characteristics, and what might explain them.

Ultimately, the findings suggest that understanding autism may require looking beyond the average brain and paying closer attention to the distinctive ways individuals process the world.

Still, Trump’s longtime adviser Marc Beckman previously teased that the docuseries, now streaming on Amazon’s Prime Video, would be a “total different experience, completely fresh.”.

Speaking to The Hollywood Reporter ahead of the Melania: The Series premiere, Beckman explained how the filmmaking team determined what would go in the documentary and what would be for the series.

“We decided that we would bifurcate and isolate certain stories that we thought were suitable for the series that weren’t necessarily appropriate for the film,” Beckman said. “The reason they’re suitable for the series is because it gives us more time to unpack more of her storyline, more about her family, more about her career, more about philanthropy and also what happens right after the inauguration when she takes on the role of being first lady of the United States again.”.

Melania: The Series producer Fernando Sulichin, who took on the same role on the documentary, added that the film “was about going into the inauguration, and this one is first lady in action and what she’s about, more intimate — not the preparation of becoming the first lady but being the first lady.”.

Beckman likened the approach to what Trump’s team did with her 2024 self-titled memoir Melania.

“With the trade edition of the book, we tell the story and we have certain photos in it, and then the collector’s edition, it’s a completely different experience so the fans could get both and enjoy them,” he noted. “That’s the same thing here.”.

Though it was initially expected that the docuseries would arrive on Amazon’s Prime Video when the documentary began streaming in March, Beckman stated that was “just the media speculating,” and insisted the timing of the series’ release was in keeping with the licensing deal with Amazon he negotiated for the film and series.

Industry observers note that “The timing for the contract is exactly what we’ve done,” he told THR on the black carpet Thursday night. “I negotiated the contract, so trust me, there’s no delay.”.

While the documentary film, which was released in theaters in late January, followed Trump in the two weeks leading up to the start of her husband’s second term as president, the docuseries, in which Trump answers softball questions about her daily routine, interests and beliefs, first focuses on her role as a wife and mother, including her relationship with the president, followed by an episode centered around her and the president’s trips to North Carolina in the wake of Hurricane Helene and Los Angeles after the 2025 wildfires.

And while the Lincoln Center screening boasted Trump’s signature black-and-white color palette, complete with a black carpet and white tables and flowers, as well as tickets and popcorn boxes featuring the first lady’s face, Beckman steered questions about a possible lifestyle firm back to Trump’s humanitarian efforts, specifically her work brokering a ceasefire in Oleshky, Ukraine and her Fostering the Future initiative to provide resources and educational opportunities for foster kids.

According to recent reports, “I think right now what she’s really proud of is how she’s helping children and people throughout the world,” Beckman remarked. “What she’s doing in America is so much more notable than a lifestyle brand.”.

And before the docuseries premiered, Trump spoke, from a black-and-white podium bearing her name, about the Ukraine ceasefire, connecting it to her own personal ethos and the series’ focus, and episode titles, of “Family & Trust” and “Pride & Honor.”.

It has been revealed that “We live in a world that never stops moving, but life’s greatest moments belong to those who can stand still,” she began. “In calmness, we can see beauty. In peace, we can see humanity. My work is demanding, and sometimes the challenges I face seem impossible. Still, even in the most difficult circumstances, I find the drive to achieve the impossible. I rely on my own strength and character, with conviction, courage and reckless determination. I found a way forward where others would not.”.

“For a brief moment, the world stood still for Oleshky. Eight hundred lives were saved. After so many years of fighting, the ceasefire brought a little bit of sunshine into lives which had been in the shadows of fear and war. The moment was very powerful for me because fighting and conflict have no value to the families on either side. Peace is rational,” she continued. “In the Oleshky ceasefire, we see the power of family, the restoration of trust and the courage of young children who do not back down in the face of war. Family, trust, pride, honor are the values we all hold in our hearts; they are also the foundation of the personal story I’m going to share with you tonight as part of Melania: The Series.”.

As Trump teased that the series offered the opportunity to “experience [her] world through a upcoming lens,” Trump’s current and former colleagues noted they hoped the show, like the documentary, let Trump tell her own story.

President Trump’s first-term adviser Kellyanne Conway said conceptually that the documentary and series were “so amazing.”.

Industry observers note that “She’s obviously a very private person who has a very public life and in my view a very positive impact and that story does not get told,” Conway told THR. “And that’s OK, so let her tell her own story.”.

Fashion designer Hervé Pierre, who created the first lady’s inaugural gowns for the president’s first and second ceremonies, added, “She’s not mysterious, but she’s not all over the media all the time and I think when she does something like she just did with [Russia and Ukraine], it’s not, like, fluff. It’s a very specific mission. So I think it’s crucial. I hope we will discover something that we don’t know about her. And I think sometimes it’s better for her to [express something in her own words] than to have an interpretation of what she’s doing. At least you have a direct line.”.

And what sort of things might viewers discover about Trump that they don’t already know?

Pierre, who’s long worked with the first lady, offered a couple of insights.

Industry observers note that “She cries when she laughs,” he said of her tendency to tear up at humorous moments. “She’s very happy. I’ve worked with difficult women for 30 years in haute couture. She never, ever raised her voice or [had attitude]. She’s always in a good mood — it’s fascinating.”.

Philanthropist Rick Baker and Blank Rome tax expert Sean Weissbart offer inspiration and advice on navigating the season of giving on Variety's 'Strictly Business' podcast.

Rick Baker is a wealth management expert by profession, advising many of Hollywood’s A-list on managing the money and portfolios for the long term in a volatile industry.

According to recent reports, for Baker himself, the concept of wealth management means giving some of it away through a scholarship program that he introduced more than 10 years ago in his hometown in rural Alabama. On the latest episode of Variety‘s “Strictly Business” podcast, as we ease into the winter holidays, Baker offers an inspirational story of how those with means can get started making a difference in the lives of others. And Sean Weissbart, a tax expert and partner at Blank Rome in Latest York, explains some significant changes to charitable giving federal tax rules that take effect for 2026.

LISTEN to the full “Strictly Business” podcast here.

It has been revealed that baker’s own life has been a fist-pumping story of a person from humble means seizing the opportunity through education after he received a scholarship to Alabama’s Auburn University. That set him on a path to building a tony wealth management practice in Beverly Hills over the past 35 years and counting. Baker has never forgotten the hard times he experienced growing up on a small farm in Crossville, Ala.

Sources indicate that “I grew up in rural Alabama with two parents who were Depression kids. My dad could not read or write,” says Baker, who is today a managing director and wealth management advisor and portfolio manager with Merrill / Bank of America.

In a recent development, “I was fortunate enough to get an academic scholarship to Auburn University, and then later I attended the Wharton Business School. During that path, I learned firsthand how important education was. And so I decided to go back and start giving back in my hometown of Crossville, Alabama. A very, very rural community, about 3,000 in population. It has one red light that’s actually not even a red light. It’s a blinking yellow light. And I go back and I try to do things that will change that community and make it better and just pay it forward,” he states.

The foundation issues scholarships for secondary education tuition. It also has a mechanism to support local youth for food, housing and transportation costs that can stand in the way of the student attending school. Baker can’t hide his emotion in explaining what it means to be able to help remove even small obstacles to achievement for underprivileged kids.
